title: Requests and company
intro: The last unit of A1 adds the imperative, for asking and telling people to do things (*Gel!*, Come!, *Oturun, lütfen*, Please sit down), and three kinds of small words that link a sentence together: *ile* (with, by), *için* (for), and the conjunctions *ve, ama, veya, ya da*. With them you can invite someone in, order in a café and say who you're going with.

blocks.text: The imperative (*emir kipi*) tells or asks someone to do something. To one person you'd call *sen*, it is the bare verb stem, with no ending: *Gel!* (Come!) *Otur!* (Sit down!) *Bak!* (Look!) *Dinle!* (Listen!)

To several people, or to one person you'd call *siz*, add `-(y)In`, in four-way harmony: *Gelin!* *Oturun!* *Bakın!* After a vowel a buffer y comes first: *Dinleyin!* *Okuyun!* The longer `-(y)InIz` is the formal form of signs, forms and announcements: *Lütfen bekleyiniz* (Please wait).

**The negative** adds `-mA` to the stem: *Gelme!* (Don't come!) *Korkma!* (Don't be afraid!) *Unutma!* (Don't forget!) Before `-(y)In`, the vowel of `-mA` takes the buffer y: *Gelmeyin*, *Korkmayın*, *Unutmayın*.

**Stem changes.** The verbs that change before `-(I)yor` in [unit 6](gp-present-continuous) change before `-(y)In` too: *git-* and *et-* soften to *gidin* and *edin* (*Yardım edin!*, Help!), and *ye-* gives *yiyin*. The bare stem stays as it is: *Git!* *Ye!* *Yardım et!*

**How polite?** The bare stem is for friends, family and children. To a stranger, a customer or an older person, use `-(y)In`. *Lütfen* (please) softens either, before or after: *Lütfen oturun*, *Oturun, lütfen*. Even so, a command can sound abrupt; softer requests such as *Bakar mısınız?*, said to call a waiter, come with the aorist in [A2](gp-aorist-uses).

items.note: formal, on a sign or a screen

blocks.title: Buyurun
blocks.text: *Buyurun* is the polite imperative of *buyurmak*, an old verb for **to command**. Turks say it when they hand you something, invite you in, or ask what you'd like: **here you are**, **come in**, **go ahead**, **how can I help?** To a friend: *Buyur*.
*İçin!* is also the polite imperative of *içmek*, **drink!**: *Çayınızı için* (Drink your tea). It looks just like *için* (for) of this unit; the sentence tells you which.

*İle* means **with**, **by** or **and**. It can stand as a separate word, *annem ile* (with my mother), but it is usually attached as a suffix, `-(y)lA`, in two-way harmony: *annemle*, *otobüsle*, *kalemle*. After a vowel a buffer y comes first: *arabayla*, *metroyla*, *Ayşe'yle*.

It covers three meanings. **Together with**: *Annemle sinemaya gidiyorum* (I'm going to the cinema with my mother). **By means of**, for transport and tools: *Okula otobüsle gidiyorum* (I go to school by bus), *Kalemle yazıyorum* (I'm writing with a pen). And **and**, between two nouns: *Ali ile Ayşe* (Ali and Ayşe). *Birlikte* (together) often follows the first meaning: *Ayşe'yle birlikte*.

**Pronouns.** The singular pronouns, and *biz* and *siz*, take the genitive before *ile*, as with *için* below: *benimle* (with me), *seninle*, *onunla*, *bizimle*, *sizinle*. *Onlar* doesn't: *onlarla*. Likewise *bununla* (with this) and *kiminle* (with whom), but *neyle* (with what, how).

items.en: I'm going to the cinema with my mother.
We go to work by metro.
We eat the cake with a fork.
Ali and Ayşe are at home.

blocks.text: `-(y)lA` starts with a consonant, so it never softens the stem: *kitapla*, *uçakla*, *çocukla*. And *şekerle* (with sugar) is not *şekerli* (sweetened), a different word you'll meet in A2.
In speech you'll also hear *bizle* and *sizle* for *bizimle* and *sizinle*. In writing, use the forms with the genitive.

*İçin* means **for**. It is a separate word and never changes. After nouns and names it simply follows: *annem için* (for my mother), *Ayşe için*, *Türkiye için*, *çocuklar için*. After the singular pronouns, *biz*, *siz*, *bu*, *şu* and *kim*, it takes the genitive, as *ile* does: *benim için*, *bunun için*, *kimin için*. But *onlar* and *ne* stay as they are: *onlar için*, *ne için* (what for).

items.en: These flowers are for my mother.
I'm tired, that's why I'm at home.

blocks.text: *İçin* after a verb, **in order to** (*öğrenmek için*, in order to learn), comes with the verbal nouns of [B1](b1-u04).
For a length of time, Turkish usually needs no *için*: *İki gün kalıyorum* (I'm staying for two days). Keep *için* for a person or a purpose: *Bu oda misafir için* (This room is for guests).

sections.title: Ve, ama, ya da: linking words

blocks.text: *Ve* (and), *ama* and *fakat* (but), *veya* and *ya da* (or) join words, phrases and sentences, much as in English: *çay ve simit* (tea and simit), *küçük ama güzel* (small but nice), *pazartesi veya salı* (Monday or Tuesday).

**Or in a question.** To ask someone to choose, Turkish puts *mI* after each option instead of using *veya*: *Çay mı, kahve mi?* (Tea or coffee?) *Bugün mü geliyorsun, yarın mı?* (Are you coming today or tomorrow?) *Çay veya kahve istiyor musunuz?*, with *veya*, asks whether you want a drink at all.

**And** has two other partners: *ile* between two nouns (*Ali ile Ayşe*), and *dA* (too) of [unit 4](gp-de-also), which often does the work of **and also**: *Ben çay istiyorum, Ayşe de kahve istiyor* (I want tea, and Ayşe wants coffee).

items.tr: Cumartesi sinemaya ya da müzeye gidiyoruz.
items.seg: Cumartesi sinema|y|a ya da müze|y|e gid|iyor|uz.
items.en: On Saturday we're going to the cinema or to a museum.

items.tr: Elif'in bir kedisi ve bir köpeği var.
items.en: Elif has a cat and a dog.

blocks.text: *Ama* is the everyday **but**; *fakat* and *ancak* sound more written. A comma before them is common but not required.

summary: Imperative: the bare stem to one friend (*gel, otur, oku*), `-(y)In` to several people or politely (*gelin, oturun, okuyun*), `-(y)InIz` on signs (*bekleyiniz*).
Negative: `-mA` (*gelme, korkma*), with y before `-(y)In`: *gelmeyin, korkmayın*. *Git-* and *et-* soften (*gidin, edin*), *ye-* gives *yiyin*.
`-(y)lA` means with, by or and: *annemle, otobüsle, arabayla, Ayşe'yle*. It never softens the stem.
Pronouns take the genitive before *ile* and *için*: *benimle, onunla, benim için, bunun için*; but *onlarla*, *onlar için*.
*Ve, ama, fakat, veya, ya da* link words and sentences. A choice in a question takes two *mI*: *Çay mı, kahve mi?*
